reason: The court held that a declaration-of-title decree binds only parties to that action, contrasting it with in-rem partition decrees.
The proposition was applied, but the supplied quote is a quotation from another case and the cited Civil Procedure Code section was not the provision construed for the rule.
The court directly held that the commissioner failed to comply with Partition Law section 32 requirements in preparing the partition scheme.
The conclusion is case-specific and omits the permit-holder and state-land basis, while SRC001 section 2 was not the provision construed for this presumption.
The court relied on the description-over-extent principle to dismiss the appeal on the boundary and encroachment issue.
The statement omits the material condition that the prescribed portion must be identifiable and found by the District Court.
The holding was under Food Act section 20(1)(b), but the supplied quote is framed as a contention and the statute id points to the Prescription Ordinance.
The burden ruling was confined to the appellants' asserted change in land condition in the acquisition-valuation context, which the statement does not preserve.
The court applied Trusts Ordinance section 83 and held no constructive trust arose where the circumstances showed an outright transfer of beneficial interest.
The court held that mere walking over a footpath without an adverse act cannot establish a prescriptive right of way under section 3.
The court rejected the alleged retransfer condition because the deed was an outright transfer and the plaintiff led no clear evidence of such a condition.
The court applied section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance and treated the quoted statutory wording as defining adverse possession.
The court applied the principle, but the supplied support is a quotation from Sri Lanka Ports Authority v Jugolinija-Boal East rather than the court's own holding.
The judgment required the party relying on impeached deeds to prove execution, not the party alleging forgery, and the relevant provision was not Evidence Ordinance section 114.
The court held that a party to a pending partition action may transfer the entitlement that will vest on final decree despite section 66.
The court held that the defective proxy should have been allowed to be rectified instead of dismissing the action.
The court expressly answered that the plaintiff could maintain the present action without depositing the deed consideration and interest.
The statement omits that ownership followed both a statutory determination and its Gazette publication in the Land Reform Law setting.
The court held the deeds void because the executant lacked the capacity or intention needed for consensus ad idem.
The court accepted inherent procedural power, but the supplied quote is from commentary and omits the absence-of-express-provision limitation.
The rule says mere ingratitude, but the court and statute required gross ingratitude and observed statutory time and court-order conditions.
The section 69 reasonable-time discussion was not the decisive holding because the appeal was resolved on actual possession and section 68(3).
The court adopted the cited authorities and itself stated that a rei vindicatio plaintiff must prove ownership and clear identity of the land.
The court construed Civil Procedure Code section 395 and held that the substituted party was bound by the original party's arrangements before court.
The case-specific trust conclusion omits the material reasons that any section 83 trust would benefit B.A. Lionel rather than the plaintiff and that the later purchaser was bona fide.
